paras: The killing of Eli Hilson was the ambush shooting of a Black farmer near Brookhaven, Lincoln County, Mississippi, on the evening of December 19, 1903, after he refused a whitecap order to leave his land. Papers in Mississippi and beyond reported him as the second Black man murdered by whitecaps in that part of the county within a month. Nearly a year later Oscar Franklin, charged by the Lincoln County Law and Order League, pleaded guilty to the murder and was sentenced to life imprisonment.

Hilson owned a farm about seven or eight miles from Brookhaven, and the local Leader described him as prosperous. Whitecaps warned him the previous winter to leave, and he disregarded the warning. On a Saturday night in late November 1903 they "literally riddled his house with bulets," according to the Leader, while his wife lay in bed with an infant a few hours old; no one was hit. Days later whitecaps fatally shot Henry List, a Black farmer in the Gum Grove neighborhood who had also been told to leave.

On Saturday, December 19, Hilson drove a young daughter into Brookhaven to spend Christmas with his brother, G. N. W. Wilson. Returning alone between sunset and dark, he was shot about a quarter of a mile from home, the bullet entering near the ear and leaving at the mouth. The horse went on home, and Hilson was found dead in the buggy. On Monday a coroner's jury found that he died of a gunshot wound "at the hands of parties unknown."

The Leader reported that Black residents had been frightened out of one neighborhood, leaving white landowners without labor, and the Baltimore Afro-American said they were "deserting the county." In November 1904 the Law and Order League's executive committee swore out an affidavit charging Will and Oscar Franklin, already jailed for the List killing, with the murder. At Oscar Franklin's preliminary hearing, Dave Posey testified that Franklin told him he had shot Hilson from behind a tree, and two women said they met Franklin carrying a gun near the spot. Four witnesses swore Franklin admitted the killing, and he was held for the grand jury.

At the December circuit court Oscar Franklin pleaded guilty and accepted a life sentence, while Will Franklin pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the List case. On December 20, 1904, Judge Wilkinson formally sentenced Oscar Franklin to life and five men to fifty years each for the List killing. No report was found of how the complicity charge against Will Franklin in the Hilson case ended.

The Brookhaven Leader ran the news under "Eli Hilson Assassinated" with an editorial calling it "a disgraceful state of affairs" and urging that "these dastardly white cap outrages" be suppressed. Its case rested mainly on lost farm labor and lenders' alarm, with "considerations of humanity" mentioned in passing.

A Brookhaven special to the Memphis Commercial-Appeal spread by wire from December 22 to Birmingham, Wichita, Butte, Corinth and Sauk Centre. Its headlines centered Hilson's refusal to go, from "Negro Disregarded the Notice and Was Slain" to "Murder Negro Who Would Not Leave." A Wichita Eagle editorial remarked that he "thought he was living in a republic, but his neighbors fooled him."

The only Black paper found reporting the killing at the time, the Baltimore Afro-American, ran a New Orleans dispatch under "Murdered by White Caps," calling Hilson "colored" and adding that Black residents were leaving. The 1904 sentences drew wider notice, under "Lynchers Get Full Penalty" in the San Francisco Call and "Long Term to Whitecappers" in the Chicago Broad Ax, which quoted the judge's vow to punish whitecappers "even if it made every woman in Mississippi a widow." The Savannah Tribune also carried the sentencing report.

The Leader and sworn 1904 testimony date the killing Saturday, December 19, while wire versions say "yesterday" under December 21 or 22 datelines and the Afro-American says Sunday; the local account, written after the inquest, is the closer source. The Leader described a shot through the head, but Dave Posey testified that Franklin said he shot Hilson in the back. One Associated Press version called Hilson the "third" such victim rather than the second.

reader.title: Killing of Eli Hilson
bases: Hilson was shot from ambush after disregarding a whitecap order to leave his farm and a night attack on his house, part of a whitecap campaign against Black residents of Lincoln County (A1, A6, A13).

Hilson was killed by whitecaps enforcing an order that he leave, a racial campaign the Leader tied to driving Black labor out of the county (A6, A10); the papers attribute the killing to the whitecap organization, but testimony and the guilty plea name a single gunman, Oscar Franklin, with his brother Will charged with complicity (A14, A15, A16).
The local Leader, the Commercial-Appeal wire and the Baltimore Afro-American agree on the ambush killing (A4, A6, A10), and the 1904 hearing and guilty plea confirm it (A14, A16, A18).
